newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland deserves a credit rating upgrade - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Poland deserves a credit rating upgrade - analysts.

text.p: Poland deserves a credit rating rise of one grade from the world's leading rating agencies ahead of its planned international bond issue in mid-1997, analysts said on Friday.

Moody's gave Poland a Baa3 investment grade in 1995 and has not changed it since, Standard & Poor's upgraded Poland to investment grade BBB minus last year from a speculative BB and IBCA also raised Poland to investment grade BBB.

"My feeling is that Poland does deserve an upgrade. It would not be unprecedented if Poland got a two point rise, but a one tick rise is more likely," said Andrew Kenningham, analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.
Last week the finance ministry said teams from rating agencies would review Poland's economy during a series of routine talks in April and May stressing no rating change had to automatically follow.
Poland plans to issue up to $500 million international bonds this year, likely at the turn of June and July for the U.S. or Japanese markets

Analysts said Poland was likely to get praise for falling inflation -- at 17.3 percent year-on-year in February against 18.5 percent in 1996 -- and last year's low budget deficit of 2.4 percent of gross domesctic product.
"I think a one tick rise for Poland would be in order. We are likely to get a plus for falling inflation and the deficit-to-GDP ratio," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING Bank in Warsaw.
"I don't know how the agencies will view progress in privatisation and we are likely to get a minus for the widening trade gap," he said.

But analysts said Poland's trade gap, at about one percent of GDP in 1996 and seen at about 3.5 percent this year, was no cause for concern in a developing economy and should not negatively influence the rating.
"The trade deficit is not big at all for a developing economy growing at the rate Poland is growing," said Tomasz Bonecki-Duda, analyst at Creditanstalt Securities in Warsaw.
Analysts said the potential rating upgrade would likely bost demand for Polish paper among foreign investors, many of whom had strict rules as to what grade they can invest their funds in.
"A higher rating would entail much lower spreads over comparable U.S. treasuries and lower costs of debt financing," said ING's Rybinski.
But others said the potential upgrade may have already been priced in by the markets so it would have little effect on spreads if or when it actually takes place.
"An upgrade may have a very limited impact on the spread over U.S. treasuries, because the markets are already anticipating a rating upgrade," said Merril Lynch's Kenningham.
